author: Adam Lindsay Gordon
blurb: Australian bush poet and horseman, celebrated for galloping ballads of riding and colonial life. His 'Bush Ballads and Galloping Rhymes' gave early Australia a poetic voice, and he is honoured with a memorial in Westminster Abbey.

author: Alan Seeger
blurb: American poet who joined the French Foreign Legion at the outbreak of the First World War. He is remembered for 'I Have a Rendezvous with Death', written shortly before he was killed in action at the Somme.

author: Alexander Pope
blurb: Master of the heroic couplet and the leading English poet of the early eighteenth century. Works like 'The Rape of the Lock' and 'An Essay on Man' made him one of the most quoted poets in the language.

author: Algernon Charles Swinburne
blurb: Victorian poet whose musical, rebellious verse scandalised and dazzled his contemporaries. His 'Poems and Ballads' brought a new sensuality and metrical daring to English poetry.

author: Ambrose Bierce
blurb: American Civil War veteran, journalist, and satirist with a famously dark wit. Best known for 'The Devil's Dictionary', he vanished without a trace in Mexico around 1914.

author: Amy Levy
blurb: Victorian poet and novelist, among the first Jewish women to study at Cambridge. Her spare, melancholy lyrics won the admiration of Oscar Wilde before her death at twenty-seven.

author: Amy Lowell
blurb: American poet from Boston who became a leading champion of the Imagist movement. She was awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry posthumously in 1926.

author: Andrew Marvell
blurb: English Metaphysical poet who also served as a Member of Parliament. 'To His Coy Mistress' and 'The Garden' are among the most celebrated lyric poems of the seventeenth century.

author: Ann Taylor
blurb: English writer of verse for children in collaboration with her sister Jane. Their joint collections, including 'Original Poems for Infant Minds', were beloved throughout the nineteenth century.

author: Anne Bradstreet
blurb: The first poet of England's American colonies to be published. Her collection 'The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America' appeared in 1650.

author: Anne Bronte
blurb: The youngest of the Brontë sisters, a poet and novelist of quiet, steady conviction. Alongside her verse she wrote the novels 'Agnes Grey' and 'The Tenant of Wildfell Hall'.

author: Anne Killigrew
blurb: English poet and painter at the court of Charles II, dead of smallpox at twenty-five. John Dryden memorialised her in one of the great elegiac odes in English.

author: Anne Kingsmill Finch
blurb: Countess of Winchilsea and one of the finest women poets of her age. Her nature poem 'A Nocturnal Reverie' was later singled out for praise by Wordsworth.

author: Annie Louisa Walker
blurb: English-born poet who spent part of her life in Canada and later published as Annie Louisa Coghill. She is best remembered for the hymn 'Work, for the Night Is Coming'.

author: Arthur Hugh Clough
blurb: Victorian poet whose questioning, sceptical verse anticipated modern doubts. Matthew Arnold mourned him in the elegy 'Thyrsis', and his 'Say not the Struggle nought Availeth' is still widely quoted.

author: Ben Jonson
blurb: Playwright and poet who dominated the literary life of Jacobean London alongside his friend Shakespeare. Lyrics like 'Song to Celia' — 'Drink to me only with thine eyes' — set the standard for classical elegance in English.

author: Charles Kingsley
blurb: Victorian clergyman, novelist, and poet. The author of 'The Water-Babies' and 'Westward Ho!' also wrote vigorous ballads and songs.

author: Charles Sorley
blurb: Scottish poet killed at the Battle of Loos at twenty. His posthumous 'Marlborough and Other Poems' marked him as one of the great losses of the First World War.

author: Charlotte Bronte
blurb: The eldest surviving Brontë sister and the author of 'Jane Eyre'. Her first appearance in print was in 'Poems by Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell', published with her sisters in 1846.

author: Charlotte Mew
blurb: English poet whose spare, dramatic lyrics won the admiration of Thomas Hardy and Virginia Woolf. 'The Farmer's Bride' is her best-known collection.

author: Charlotte Smith
blurb: English poet and novelist who led the revival of the sonnet in the late eighteenth century. Her 'Elegiac Sonnets' influenced both Wordsworth and Coleridge.

author: Christina Rossetti
blurb: One of the great Victorian poets and sister of the painter Dante Gabriel Rossetti. 'Goblin Market' and the carol 'In the Bleak Midwinter' are among her best-loved works.

author: Christopher Marlowe
blurb: Elizabethan playwright and poet, Shakespeare's most gifted contemporary, killed in a tavern quarrel at twenty-nine. 'The Passionate Shepherd to His Love' is one of the most imitated lyrics in English.

author: Christopher Smart
blurb: Eighteenth-century English poet confined for years in an asylum, where he wrote the visionary 'Jubilate Agno'. His 'A Song to David' is considered a masterpiece of religious poetry.

author: Claude McKay
blurb: Jamaican-born poet and novelist, a central figure of the Harlem Renaissance. His sonnet 'If We Must Die' became an anthem of resistance and dignity.

author: Coventry Patmore
blurb: Victorian poet associated with the Pre-Raphaelite circle. His long poem 'The Angel in the House', a celebration of married love, gave the era one of its most debated phrases.

author: D. H. Lawrence
blurb: English novelist and poet, author of 'Sons and Lovers' and 'Women in Love'. His free-verse poems of animals and the natural world, such as 'Snake', are among his most admired writing.

author: Edgar Allan Poe
blurb: American master of the macabre in both verse and story. 'The Raven' made him famous, while 'Annabel Lee' and 'The Bells' show his hypnotic command of sound.

author: Edmund Spenser
blurb: Elizabethan poet of 'The Faerie Queene', the great allegorical epic of the age. The Spenserian stanza he invented shaped English poetry for centuries.

author: Edna St. Vincent Millay
blurb: American lyric poet and playwright, famous in the 1920s for her wit and candour. She won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1923.

author: Edward Fitzgerald
blurb: English writer remembered for one of poetry's most beloved translations. His free rendering of 'The Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám' became a Victorian sensation.

author: Edward Lear
blurb: English artist and the master of nonsense verse. 'The Owl and the Pussy-Cat' and his limericks have delighted readers for more than a century and a half.

author: Edward Taylor
blurb: Puritan minister of colonial Massachusetts whose intricate devotional poems went unpublished for two centuries. Their rediscovery in the 1930s revealed one of colonial America's finest poets.

author: Edward Thomas
blurb: English writer who turned to poetry only in his final years, encouraged by his friend Robert Frost. Killed at Arras in 1917, he left poems like 'Adlestrop' that distil the English countryside.

author: Eliza Cook
blurb: Self-taught English poet, hugely popular with Victorian working-class readers. Her sentimental favourite 'The Old Arm-Chair' was known in households across Britain and America.

author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
blurb: One of the most celebrated poets of the Victorian era. Her 'Sonnets from the Portuguese', written for her husband Robert Browning, include 'How do I love thee? Let me count the ways'.

author: Emily Bronte
blurb: Author of 'Wuthering Heights' and the most powerful poet among the Brontë sisters. Visionary lyrics like 'No coward soul is mine' stand with the era's best.

author: Emily Dickinson
blurb: Reclusive poet of Amherst, Massachusetts, who published almost nothing in her lifetime. Her nearly 1,800 compressed, startling poems reshaped American literature after her death.

author: Emma Lazarus
blurb: American poet and advocate for Jewish refugees. Her sonnet 'The New Colossus' — 'Give me your tired, your poor' — is engraved at the Statue of Liberty.

author: Ernest Dowson
blurb: English poet of the Decadent 1890s, dead at thirty-two. His verse gave the language the phrases 'gone with the wind' and 'days of wine and roses'.

author: Eugene Field
blurb: American journalist known as the poet of childhood. 'Wynken, Blynken, and Nod' and 'Little Boy Blue' made him a household name.

author: Francis Thompson
blurb: English Catholic poet rescued from opium addiction and homelessness by his publishers. His masterpiece 'The Hound of Heaven' depicts God's relentless pursuit of the soul.

author: Geoffrey Chaucer
blurb: The father of English poetry and the first great writer in the English vernacular. 'The Canterbury Tales' remains one of the funniest and most humane works in literature.

author: George Eliot
blurb: Pen name of Mary Ann Evans, one of the greatest Victorian novelists. Alongside 'Middlemarch' she wrote thoughtful verse, including the long poem 'The Spanish Gypsy'.

author: George Gordon, Lord Byron
blurb: The most famous — and infamous — of the Romantic poets, 'mad, bad, and dangerous to know'. 'Don Juan' and 'Childe Harold's Pilgrimage' made him a European celebrity, and he died supporting Greek independence.

author: George Herbert
blurb: Welsh-born priest and Metaphysical poet of quiet devotion. His single collection, 'The Temple', contains some of the finest religious lyrics in English.

author: George Meredith
blurb: Victorian novelist and poet. His sonnet sequence 'Modern Love' dissected a failing marriage with startling candour for its time.

author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
blurb: Jesuit priest whose 'sprung rhythm' and ecstatic nature poems were unknown until published in 1918. 'The Windhover' and 'Pied Beauty' now rank among the most original poems in English.

author: Helen Hunt Jackson
blurb: American poet, campaigner for Native American rights, and childhood friend of Emily Dickinson. Her novel 'Ramona' and report 'A Century of Dishonor' stirred the nation's conscience.

author: Henry David Thoreau
blurb: American Transcendentalist and author of 'Walden' and 'Civil Disobedience'. His poems carry the same close attention to nature and conscience as his prose.

author: Henry Vaughan
blurb: Welsh Metaphysical poet and physician. His visionary collection 'Silex Scintillans' includes 'The World', which opens 'I saw Eternity the other night'.

author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
blurb: The most popular American poet of the nineteenth century. 'Paul Revere's Ride', 'The Song of Hiawatha', and 'Evangeline' were recited in parlours across the world.

author: Hugh Henry Brackenridge
blurb: Scottish-born American writer and jurist who founded the Pittsburgh Gazette. With Philip Freneau he co-wrote the patriotic poem 'The Rising Glory of America'.

author: Isaac Watts
blurb: English minister called the father of English hymnody. He wrote some 750 hymns, including 'Joy to the World' and 'O God, Our Help in Ages Past'.

author: James Henry Leigh Hunt
blurb: English essayist, editor, and poet at the centre of Romantic literary life, a friend to Keats and Shelley. 'Abou Ben Adhem' and 'Jenny Kiss'd Me' keep his verse alive.

author: James Thomson
blurb: Scottish poet whose long poem 'The Seasons' pioneered nature poetry in English. He also wrote the words to 'Rule, Britannia!'.

author: James Weldon Johnson
blurb: American writer, diplomat, and civil-rights leader of the Harlem Renaissance era. He wrote 'Lift Every Voice and Sing', often called the Black national anthem.

author: James Whitcomb Riley
blurb: The 'Hoosier Poet', beloved for dialect verse of small-town Indiana. 'Little Orphant Annie' and 'When the Frost Is on the Punkin' made him America's favourite poet of his day.

author: Jane Austen
blurb: England's great novelist of manners also wrote playful occasional verse for family and friends. Her poems share the wit that animates 'Pride and Prejudice' and 'Emma'.

author: Jane Taylor
blurb: English poet who wrote for children with her sister Ann. Her poem 'The Star' gave the world 'Twinkle, twinkle, little star'.

author: John Clare
blurb: English farm labourer turned poet, with an unmatched eye for the countryside. Celebrated, then neglected, and writing on through years in an asylum, he is now ranked among the great Romantic poets.

author: John Donne
blurb: The greatest of the Metaphysical poets and Dean of St Paul's Cathedral. From 'The Flea' to 'Death, be not proud', his poems fuse passion and intellect like no other.

author: John Dryden
blurb: England's first officially appointed Poet Laureate and the dominant literary figure of the Restoration. His satires, translations, and criticism set the course for the century that followed.

author: John Greenleaf Whittier
blurb: American Quaker poet and fervent abolitionist. His winter idyll 'Snow-Bound' was one of the era's best-selling poems.

author: John Keats
blurb: English Romantic who wrote 'Ode to a Nightingale', 'To Autumn', and 'Ode on a Grecian Urn' before dying of tuberculosis at twenty-five. His odes and letters are cornerstones of English poetry.

author: John McCrae
blurb: Canadian physician and soldier of the First World War. He wrote 'In Flanders Fields', the poem that made the poppy a symbol of remembrance.

author: John Milton
blurb: Author of 'Paradise Lost', the English epic of Satan's rebellion and humanity's fall, composed after he had gone completely blind. He stands with Shakespeare at the summit of English letters.

author: John Trumbull
blurb: American poet and judge, one of the 'Connecticut Wits'. His mock epic 'M'Fingal' satirised Loyalists during the Revolution.

author: John Wilmot
blurb: The Earl of Rochester, the most notorious wit and libertine of Charles II's court. His satires and lyrics combine scandalous frankness with brilliant craft; he died at thirty-three.

author: Jonathan Swift
blurb: Anglo-Irish satirist, author of 'Gulliver's Travels', and Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin. His verse shares the savage wit of his prose.

author: Joseph Warton
blurb: English critic, poet, and headmaster of Winchester College. With his brother Thomas he helped turn eighteenth-century taste away from wit and towards imagination and nature.

author: Joyce Kilmer
blurb: American poet killed in action in France in the First World War. His poem 'Trees' — 'I think that I shall never see / A poem lovely as a tree' — became one of America's most recited.

author: Julia Ward Howe
blurb: American writer, abolitionist, and suffragist. She wrote 'The Battle Hymn of the Republic' in 1861, and it became the great anthem of the Union cause.

author: Jupiter Hammon
blurb: The first published African-American poet, enslaved on Long Island for his entire life. His devotional poem 'An Evening Thought' was written in 1760.

author: Katherine Philips
blurb: Poet celebrated in her day as 'the Matchless Orinda'. Her poems of female friendship made her one of the first Englishwomen to win literary fame.

author: Lady Mary Chudleigh
blurb: English poet and essayist with strikingly early feminist convictions. Her poem 'To the Ladies' declares 'Wife and servant are the same, / But only differ in the name'.

author: Lewis Carroll
blurb: Pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, Oxford mathematician and author of 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland'. 'Jabberwocky' is the most famous nonsense poem in English.

author: Lord Alfred Tennyson
blurb: Queen Victoria's Poet Laureate for more than forty years. 'The Charge of the Light Brigade', 'Ulysses', and 'In Memoriam' defined Victorian poetry.

author: Louisa May Alcott
blurb: Author of 'Little Women', raised among the Concord Transcendentalists. Her occasional poems include 'Thoreau's Flute', a moving elegy for her family's friend.

author: Major Henry Livingston, Jr.
blurb: Poet and Revolutionary War veteran of New York's Hudson Valley. Some scholars argue that he, not Clement Clarke Moore, wrote ''Twas the night before Christmas'.

author: Mark Twain
blurb: Pen name of Samuel Clemens, America's great humorist and the author of 'Adventures of Huckleberry Finn'. His rare ventures into verse carry the same sly wit.

author: Mary Elizabeth Coleridge
blurb: English poet and novelist, a great-grandniece of Samuel Taylor Coleridge. She published her admired verse under the pseudonym 'Anodos'.

author: Matthew Arnold
blurb: Victorian poet and critic, son of Rugby School's famous headmaster. 'Dover Beach' is one of the most anthologised poems of the nineteenth century.

author: Matthew Prior
blurb: English poet and diplomat who helped negotiate the Treaty of Utrecht. His light, epigrammatic verse made him a master of easy, conversational poetry.

author: Michael Drayton
blurb: Elizabethan poet of enormous range and industry. His sonnet 'Since there's no help, come let us kiss and part' is among the era's finest, and 'Poly-Olbion' mapped all of England in verse.

author: Oliver Goldsmith
blurb: Irish essayist, novelist, and playwright, author of 'The Vicar of Wakefield' and 'She Stoops to Conquer'. His poem 'The Deserted Village' mourned the decline of rural life.

author: Oliver Wendell Holmes
blurb: Boston physician, essayist, and one of the 'Fireside Poets'. 'Old Ironsides' helped save the USS Constitution, and 'The Chambered Nautilus' was a schoolroom staple for generations.

author: Oscar Wilde
blurb: Irish wit, playwright, and author of 'The Picture of Dorian Gray'. 'The Ballad of Reading Gaol', written after his imprisonment, is his poetic masterpiece.

author: Paul Laurence Dunbar
blurb: One of the first African-American poets to achieve international fame, born to formerly enslaved parents. He wrote 'We Wear the Mask' and 'Sympathy' — 'I know why the caged bird sings' — before dying at thirty-three.

author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
blurb: Radical Romantic poet, expelled from Oxford for atheism and drowned at twenty-nine off the Italian coast. 'Ozymandias', 'Ode to the West Wind', and 'To a Skylark' are among the most famous poems in English.

author: Philip Freneau
blurb: Known as the 'Poet of the American Revolution', he was also a sea captain and partisan newspaper editor. Poems like 'The Wild Honey Suckle' foreshadowed American Romanticism.

author: Phillis Wheatley
blurb: Kidnapped from West Africa and enslaved in Boston, she became the first African-American author of a published book of poetry. Her 1773 'Poems on Various Subjects' made her famous on both sides of the Atlantic.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
blurb: The sage of Concord and central figure of American Transcendentalism. His 'Concord Hymn' coined the phrase 'the shot heard round the world'.

author: Richard Crashaw
blurb: English Metaphysical poet whose fervent religious verse drew on the Catholic Baroque. 'Steps to the Temple' contains his most ecstatic devotional poetry.

author: Richard Lovelace
blurb: Cavalier poet imprisoned for his loyalty to Charles I. From prison he wrote 'To Althea': 'Stone walls do not a prison make, / Nor iron bars a cage'.

author: Robert Browning
blurb: Victorian master of the dramatic monologue in poems like 'My Last Duchess'. His elopement with Elizabeth Barrett is one of literature's great love stories.

author: Robert Burns
blurb: Scotland's national poet, the 'Ploughman Poet' of Ayrshire. 'Auld Lang Syne', 'To a Mouse', and 'A Red, Red Rose' are sung and quoted the world over.

author: Robert Herrick
blurb: Cavalier poet and country parson in Devon. 'To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time' — 'Gather ye rosebuds while ye may' — is his signature note of carpe diem.

author: Robert Louis Stevenson
blurb: Scottish author of 'Treasure Island' and 'Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde'. His 'A Child's Garden of Verses' remains a classic of children's poetry.

author: Robert Southey
blurb: English Romantic, Poet Laureate for thirty years, and friend of Coleridge and Wordsworth. He also wrote the first published version of the tale of the Three Bears.

author: Robinson
blurb: English Romantic poet, actress, and celebrity known as 'the English Sappho'. Famous first as 'Perdita' on the London stage, she became a prolific poet admired by Coleridge.

author: Rupert Brooke
blurb: English poet whose golden looks and early death made him an emblem of the First World War's lost generation. His sonnet 'The Soldier' begins 'If I should die, think only this of me'.

author: Samuel Coleridge
blurb: With Wordsworth, he launched English Romanticism in 'Lyrical Ballads'. 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner' and 'Kubla Khan' are two of the most spellbinding poems in the language.

author: Samuel Johnson
blurb: The great critic, essayist, and compiler of the 1755 'Dictionary of the English Language'. His poem 'The Vanity of Human Wishes' is among the finest verse satires of its age.

author: Sara Teasdale
blurb: American lyric poet from St. Louis, prized for her pure, songlike verse. Her collection 'Love Songs' won the 1918 prize that became the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry.

author: Sarah Flower Adams
blurb: English poet and hymn writer. Her hymn 'Nearer, My God, to Thee' is reputedly what the band played as the Titanic sank.

author: Sidney Lanier
blurb: Poet and musician of the American South who contracted tuberculosis as a prisoner in the Civil War. 'The Song of the Chattahoochee' and 'The Marshes of Glynn' show his remarkable musical ear.

author: Sir John Suckling
blurb: Cavalier poet, courtier, and gambler credited with inventing the game of cribbage. His 'Ballad upon a Wedding' typifies his easy, charming style.

author: Sir Philip Sidney
blurb: Elizabethan courtier-poet, the very model of the Renaissance gentleman, dead at thirty-one from a wound taken in battle at Zutphen. 'Astrophil and Stella' is the first great English sonnet sequence.

author: Sir Thomas Wyatt
blurb: Tudor courtier and diplomat under Henry VIII who introduced the sonnet into English. 'Whoso List to Hunt' is often read as a poem about Anne Boleyn.

author: Sir Walter Raleigh
blurb: Elizabethan adventurer, courtier, and coloniser, executed under James I. His poems, including 'The Nymph's Reply to the Shepherd', carry a worldly, sceptical grace.

author: Sir Walter Scott
blurb: Scottish author of 'Ivanhoe' and the Waverley novels, first famous as a poet. 'The Lady of the Lake' and 'Marmion' — 'O, what a tangled web we weave' — were the bestsellers of their day.

author: Stephen Crane
blurb: American author of 'The Red Badge of Courage', dead of tuberculosis at twenty-eight. His stark free-verse poems were decades ahead of their time.

author: Thomas Campbell
blurb: Scottish poet famous for stirring war songs like 'Ye Mariners of England' and 'Hohenlinden'. He was also a driving force in the founding of University College London.

author: Thomas Chatterton
blurb: Bristol prodigy who passed off his own medieval-style poems as the work of an invented monk, 'Thomas Rowley'. His death at seventeen made him Romanticism's emblem of doomed genius.

author: Thomas Flatman
blurb: English poet and celebrated miniature painter of the Restoration. His melancholy meditations on death were much admired in his day.

author: Thomas Gray
blurb: English poet and Cambridge scholar. His 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' is one of the most quoted poems in the English language.

author: Thomas Hood
blurb: English poet and humorist, a master of the pun. His 'The Song of the Shirt', on the plight of a seamstress, was a sensation of social protest.

author: Thomas Moore
blurb: Ireland's national lyricist, and the friend and biographer of Byron. His 'Irish Melodies', including 'The Last Rose of Summer', were sung across Europe.

author: Thomas Warton
blurb: Oxford professor, literary historian, and Poet Laureate from 1785. His pioneering 'History of English Poetry' recovered England's medieval literary past.

author: Walt Whitman
blurb: The great poet of American democracy. 'Leaves of Grass', expanded across his lifetime, contains 'Song of Myself' and 'O Captain! My Captain!'.

author: Walter Savage Landor
blurb: English poet famed for a fiery temper and perfectly chiselled epigrams. 'Rose Aylmer' and 'Dying Speech of an Old Philosopher' show his classical finish.

author: Wilfred Owen
blurb: The greatest English poet of the First World War, killed one week before the Armistice. 'Dulce et Decorum Est' and 'Anthem for Doomed Youth' indict what he called 'the old Lie'.

author: William Allingham
blurb: Irish poet and diarist, a friend of Tennyson and the Pre-Raphaelites. 'The Fairies' — 'Up the airy mountain, / Down the rushy glen' — is his enduring legacy.

author: William Barnes
blurb: Dorset clergyman and philologist who wrote tender poems in the Dorset dialect. Thomas Hardy revered him as a master.

author: William Blake
blurb: Visionary poet, painter, and engraver, barely noticed in his own lifetime. 'Songs of Innocence and of Experience' — including 'The Tyger' — and the lines that became the hymn 'Jerusalem' are now central to English literature.

author: William Browne
blurb: Devon pastoral poet known as William Browne of Tavistock. His 'Britannia's Pastorals' influenced Milton and Keats, and his epitaph on the Countess Dowager of Pembroke is a small classic.

author: William Butler Yeats
blurb: Ireland's greatest poet, a founder of Dublin's Abbey Theatre, and winner of the 1923 Nobel Prize in Literature. 'The Lake Isle of Innisfree' and 'The Second Coming' span his early lyricism and late visionary power.

author: William Cowper
blurb: English poet of nature and domestic life who struggled all his life with depression. His hymns include 'God Moves in a Mysterious Way', and his long poem 'The Task' influenced the Romantics.

author: William Cullen Bryant
blurb: American nature poet and, for half a century, editor of the New York Evening Post. 'Thanatopsis', drafted in his teens, announced the arrival of American poetry.

author: William Ernest Henley
blurb: English editor and poet who lost a leg to tubercular disease in his youth. From his hospital bed he wrote 'Invictus': 'I am the master of my fate: / I am the captain of my soul'.

author: William Lisle Bowles
blurb: English clergyman whose 'Fourteen Sonnets' of 1789 helped spark the Romantic sonnet revival. The young Coleridge idolised him.

author: William Morris
blurb: Victorian designer, socialist, and poet, central to the Arts and Crafts movement. 'The Earthly Paradise' made him one of the most popular poets of his era.

author: William Shakespeare
blurb: England's national poet and the world's most performed dramatist. His 154 sonnets — 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?' — are the most famous poems in English.

author: William Topaz McGonagall
blurb: Dundee weaver affectionately celebrated as the worst poet in the English language. 'The Tay Bridge Disaster' is his unforgettable masterpiece of unintentional comedy.

author: William Vaughn Moody
blurb: American poet and dramatist who taught at the University of Chicago. His 'An Ode in Time of Hesitation' questioned American imperialism; he died at forty-one.

author: William Wordsworth
blurb: The central poet of English Romanticism and Poet Laureate from 1843. 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud', 'Tintern Abbey', and 'The Prelude' made the inner life of nature his lifelong subject.
